applied.why: The drawn line is the Scatter Creek trail to Scatter Lake and the south slopes — the standard route from the south, not the north ridge from Wolf Creek.
the 7-point sketch runs through the Lightning Creek / Willow Lake / south-east buttress variant pins, not the Hozomeen Lake approach the row describes

applied.name: Lightning Creek boat landing / trail junction

applied.why: The drawn line runs from the Thunder Creek valley north of Park Creek Pass straight to pins on the NORTH side of the peak (plus a stray vertex ~13 km east); it never follows the documented route up the Park Creek trail, the washout climbers' path and the basin south of the peak.

applied.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin

waypoints.name: Wolf Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start of Wolf Creek Trail #527, at the end of a gravel Forest Service road west of Winthrop.

waypoints.name: Gardner Meadows
waypoints.note: End of the Wolf Creek Trail, about 10 miles in, and the usual camp. From the last campsites a faint path crosses Wolf Creek toward Abernathy Lake and the upper tarn. Not plotted on the map.

waypoints.name: North Ridge saddle
waypoints.note: Saddle on the north ridge crest roughly 0.6 mi north of the summit. The coordinate is an estimate, not a surveyed fix.

waypoints.name: Abernathy Peak summit
waypoints.note: High point of Abernathy Ridge.

waypoints.name: Beverly Turnpike Trailhead (#1391)
waypoints.note: South/Teanaway-side approach via Beverly Creek and Fourth Creek trails toward Ingalls Creek, then bushwhack/scramble up to the SE side of the peak. Matches this route's own recorded GPS track almost exactly.

waypoints.name: Denny Creek Trailhead (I-90 Exit 47)
waypoints.note: Start of the Denny Creek Trail #1014 toward Melakwa Lake; leave it at Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles up, for the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 47 and follow Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 to the trailhead lot at about 2,300 feet.

waypoints.name: Source Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Signed junction on Snow Lake Trail #1013; leave the main trail here and head toward Source Lake basin.

waypoints.name: Source Lake basin stream crossing
waypoints.note: Climbers' path fords the outlet stream draining Source Lake basin around 4,100 ft; last reliable water before the ascent gully, cairns mark the crossing.

waypoints.name: Gully 'secret passage' below the cliffs
waypoints.note: An easy-to-miss rock passage at ~4,780 ft where the route leaves the open streambed gully and climbs NE along cliff bands into the upper basin.

waypoints.name: Thumbtack (rock tower), upper basin
waypoints.note: Prominent free-standing rock tower marking the talus basin between Bryant and Chair Peak; from here the route corkscrews southwest toward the Bryant-Chair gully.

waypoints.name: Bryant-Chair Peak gully / talus shoulder
waypoints.note: Steep, loose gully between the two peaks gains a talus shoulder on Bryant's ridge; helmets recommended, rockfall risk from parties above.

waypoints.name: Summit block traverse
waypoints.note: Route stays left (south) of the talus field and traverses the south side of the west shoulder before the final scramble; exposed with loose rock, though holds are generally good.

waypoints.name: Lightning Creek boat landing / trail junction
waypoints.note: Water-taxi drop point on Ross Lake's east shore (~10 lake-miles north of Ross Dam); pick up the East Bank/Lightning Creek Trail here — this is mile ~16 of the SR-20 approach trail, a designated boat-in camp requiring a backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Willow Lake
waypoints.note: Small lake along the trail (~mile 20); last reliable water before leaving the maintained trail — the 1988 southeast-buttress party left the trail just beyond Willow Lake to cut east toward the peak.

waypoints.name: Off-trail brush/ravine to the 5,000-ft shoulder
waypoints.note: Cross-country push through timber and avalanche debris into a deep ravine, then steep dirt-and-brush climbing to a broad timbered shoulder and meadows near 5,000 ft, bypassing cliff bands on their west side.

waypoints.name: 6,200-ft saddle below the SE buttress
waypoints.note: Ridge saddle directly beneath the southeast buttress, used as a bivouac by the 1988 first-ascent party; no reported water — carry up from Willow Lake.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20)
waypoints.note: Park here and walk down to Ross Lake Resort for the water taxi north to the Hozomeen campground at the head of the lake, where the walk to Hozomeen Lake begins.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass / Fisher Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: On SR-20 near milepost 151, ~10-car lot with pit toilet; Northwest Forest Pass required to park.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Easy Pass/Fisher Creek Trailhead on SR-20, a marked pullout near milepost 151 about five miles west of Rainy Pass at roughly 3,700 feet elevation. The lot holds about ten cars, has a pit toilet and no water, and a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. Overnight camping requires a backcountry permit, reserved in advance through Recreation.gov or picked up as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

waypoints.name: Easy Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the Forest Service/North Cascades NP boundary here; views of Mt. Logan and Fisher Peak before the trail switchbacks down into Fisher Basin.
waypoints.directions: The Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily through forest and then open meadow and talus, gaining about 2,800 ft over three and a half miles; a fit party takes an hour and a half to two hours. Streams are reliable lower down but there is none at the pass itself, so fill up before the last switchbacks.

waypoints.name: Fisher Camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp (3 tent sites, privy) in the Fisher Creek valley with water from Fisher Creek just downhill; used as the jump-off point to leave the trail for Mesahchie's south side.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the trail switchbacks down the far side, losing roughly 1,400 ft over three miles into the Fisher Creek valley. Every foot of that has to be climbed again at the end of the trip — budget around six hours summit-to-car and do not judge the exit by how fast this descent goes.

waypoints.name: Off-trail turnoff above Fisher Camp
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Fisher Creek Trail roughly a half-mile past Fisher Camp and head upslope along the stream draining Mesahchie's southeast/south basin.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the Fisher Creek Trail for roughly another half mile past the camp, continuing gently downstream, until you reach a grassy, flower-filled glade. Nothing marks the departure and the maintained trail carries on past it, so it is worth fixing on a track; this is the last built tread of the day.

waypoints.name: 8,050 ft ridge shoulder
waypoints.note: Flat spot on the ridge at the base of the summit pyramid where the south rib meets the southwest gully system; descend a few feet south to enter the climbing gully.
waypoints.directions: Head cross-country and uphill along the drainage above the trail. Around 6,500 ft the line crosses a waterfall on an easy bench — the last reliable water, and the one real hazard on the approach, since it is slick and worse after rain or with snow still around. Above it, work up a mix of scree, talus, grass benches and low-angle blocky rock, threading short cliff bands and steep heather to a shoulder near 6,700-6,800 ft with flat bivy ground, then up the ridge crest itself, where a few Class 4 moves are needed to get established, onto gentler but loose cairned terrain. Everything above Fisher Creek is unmarked and parties do get cliffed out on this flank, so carry a GPX track or route photos rather than working from a description.

waypoints.name: Chockstone notch (crux gully)
waypoints.note: Rap-sling and cairn-marked gully narrows here; a Class 4 move past a chockstone in a notch gains the final summit ridge — very loose rock, test every hold.
waypoints.directions: Drop south off the shoulder to enter the first obvious gully on the southwest side, identifiable by its beige rock. It is steep Class 3-4 where it starts, then broadens and eases once a string of cairns appears. Follow it up until it steepens again and look left for the notch.

waypoints.name: Summit ridge crest
waypoints.note: Narrow crest with a series of small false points leading to the true summit; exposed scrambling on both sides.
waypoints.directions: The Class 4 move past the chockstone leads into a deep-cut traverse and a second gully, which runs up to the crest. The rock through here is genuinely rotten — test every hold, and keep the party out from under each other, because anything knocked loose funnels straight down the gully.

waypoints.name: Mesahchie Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Ragged Ridge's highest point; panoramic views of Mt. Logan, Goode, and the Fisher Creek/Thunder Creek drainages.
waypoints.directions: From the top of the west gully, follow the ridge crest east to the top. It is exposed but moderate, narrow and dropping away on both sides.

waypoints.name: Colonial Creek Campground Trailhead
waypoints.note: Drive-to trailhead in Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130; the Thunder Creek Trail leaves from the south end of the campground near the amphitheater. The alternative southern start is by boat to Stehekin and shuttle to High Bridge, then up the Park Creek Trail.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead, the start of the most commonly used approach into this basin. From there the Thunder Creek Trail — an easy, mostly forested stock and hiker trail — climbs only about 600 feet over its first 13 miles up-valley. Two alternate approaches reach the same high basin: a steeper, more direct line over McAlester Pass and down Rainbow Creek, also starting from SR-20, or a southern approach by boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp, then up the Park Creek Trail. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required, and if you're using the Stehekin ferry or shuttle, both run on a limited schedule — typically mid-June through September — so check timetables and reserve the permit before planning dates.

waypoints.name: Skagit Queen Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp near old Skagit Queen mine workings where the trail steepens into switchbacks; reliable creek water, common first- or second-night stop.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail south from the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 — an easy, mostly-forested stock/hiker trail with only about 600 ft of gain — roughly 13 miles up-valley, passing McAllister Camp near mile 6 and Junction Camp near mile 9.5.

waypoints.name: Park Creek Pass
waypoints.note: Trail high point in the notch between Mt. Logan and Mt. Buckner; camping is prohibited at the pass itself to protect fragile meadows, so continue on or camp just below it.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-valley past Thunder Basin Camp around mile 16.5, then pick up the signed Park Creek Pass Trail junction a couple of miles beyond; it switchbacks up through meadows to the pass.

waypoints.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
waypoints.note: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib south of Storm King with a nearby water source; leave the maintained trail here and go cross-country toward the peak.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and traverse cross-country west/southwest across snow and talus, favouring climber's left, toward the basin under Storm King's east and west towers. Carry an ice axe and consider crampons into August for lingering snow on this traverse, and take care not to drift off-line in poor visibility.

waypoints.name: Talus cirque beneath the towers
waypoints.note: About a mile of loose talus/scree past the rib camp brings you into the cirque directly under Storm King's west and east towers; take the path of least resistance up the scree.
waypoints.directions: About a mile of loose talus and scree past the rib camp, bearing right toward the cirque; cairns mark a Class 2-3 climber's trail and the line is the path of least resistance up the scree.

waypoints.name: North-side exposed ledge traverse
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 ledge system traversing the backside of the summit towers, including a slight overhang requiring a squeeze-under move; most parties fix a line here.
waypoints.directions: From the cirque, ascend the long, very loose talus/scree slope on the path of least resistance toward the southwest gully system below the summit rocks, staying right of the horn-shaped rock gully at about 8,000 ft to be in the correct gully. This slope is the approach's main hazard — helmets on and space the party out for rockfall and unstable footing. Around 70 ft of Class 3 scrambling reaches the notch, and it is the right-most of the notches in the summit rocks; cross to the north side of it to gain the ledge.

waypoints.name: Summit crux crack
waypoints.note: 15-foot crack (Class 4 to low 5th) leads to the fixed rappel anchor used for the descent; rope up or belay through this section.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the ledge roughly 70 ft across the backside of the tower — two or three Class 4 moves, full exposure, and a squeeze under a slight overhang; many parties fix a line. The ledge widens and holds loose rock, so move carefully, then continue across the summit tower's backside to the small spur at the foot of the crack.

waypoints.name: Storm King summit
waypoints.directions: Climb the 15-ft solid Class 4 face crack, or wrap around its left side on easier Class 3 blocks; both reach the register and the fixed rappel slings. A final short Class 3 pitch tops out. Two points above 8,520 ft sit east of the triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit — the easternmost is the true high point.
